# Country screening

Whether each of the nine is a defensible choice, and whether the four added
countries survive the evidence. Sources in [citations.md](../citations.md).

## The screening question that matters most

Not "can foreigners buy" — that flattens four materially different risk classes
into one. The classes are:

- **(a)** unrestricted fee-simple purchase
- **(b)** purchase subject to a **discretionary permit** that can be refused
- **(c)** a **non-fee-simple structure** — a bank trust, a concession — where the
  investor never holds title
- **(d)** an **outright bar**

A country can be all four at once depending on where the property sits. Mexico is
(a)/(b) inland and (c) on the coast. Costa Rica is (d) on the coast and unknown
inland.

## Verdicts

| Country | Instrument evidenced | Carve-out | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mexico** | Inland: permit deemed granted on 5-day silence. Restricted zone: **50-year bank trust, no rights in rem** | **100 km borders / 50 km coasts** [5] | keep, with the zone treated as a separate asset class |
| **Hungary** | **Discretionary per-property permit**, HUF 65,000, 45 days, mandatory refusal on public or municipal interest | asset-class, not geographic | keep, with an execution-risk caveat |
| **Costa Rica** | Coast: **outright bar** on non-resident foreigners and >50% foreign-owned entities. Inland: unknown | **200 m coastal strip, all islands** [7] | keep only for inland, which is unevidenced |
| **Portugal** | Acquisition right not stated; **flat 7.5% IMT on non-residents** with a long-let escape | none found | keep, with a quantified entry penalty |
| **Italy** | Reciprocity condition; **1949 FCN treaty grants national treatment on immovable property** [8]; MAECI's own determination unconfirmed | none found | keep; gate narrowed, not closed |
| **Spain** | Not stated; tax authority administers non-resident ownership routinely | none found | keep, with a severe use-side caveat in Barcelona |
| **Greece** | Not stated — all tax-authority sources blocked | none on acquisition; **use-side ban in central Athens** | keep on ownership by default only |
| **France** | Not stated | none found | **insufficient evidence** |
| **Panama** | Not stated — land authority and both gazettes failed | none found | **insufficient evidence** |

**"Insufficient evidence" means one thing: no file in this run supports a finding
either way.** It is a statement about the corpus, not about the country, and must
not be read as a negative finding about France or Panama.

## On the four additions the brief asked to stress-test

**Portugal — survives, and is the clearest case of policy moving against
non-resident buyers found anywhere in this study.** CIMT art. 17(10), added by DL
97/2026 of 20 May 2026, imposes a flat **7.5%** transfer tax on a non-resident
acquiring urban residential property, with **all exemptions and reductions
disapplied** [9][10]. It is a price, not a bar, and it has a lawful escape that
happens to fit a buy-to-let strategy: letting the property for housing within six
months at a capped rent and keeping it let at least 36 months in the first five
years. The rent cap for **this** purpose is 2.5× the 2026 statutory minimum monthly wage
(DL 97/2026 art. 2(2)(a)) [10] — and the corpus does not contain the 2026 wage
figure, so the constraint's severity cannot be quantified here.

Do not confuse that ceiling with the different one in the same decree: the
separate **accessible-rent regime (RSAA, annex iii) art. 4** sets its ceiling at
**80% of the INE median rent for the concelho** [10]. Two distinct provisions,
two distinct ceilings, two distinct purposes — the first gates the IMT escape,
the second gates an IRS and IRC exemption. See
[tenancy-law.md](tenancy-law.md). The trade-off is real: escape the surcharge by accepting a
legislated below-market rent and a multi-year letting commitment, or pay it.

**Mexico — survives, but only if the restricted zone is screened separately.**
Inland is close to ordinary fee simple with a permit that is deemed granted on
SRE silence in five business days [5]. Coastal and border property is a 50-year
renewable bank trust conferring "utilización y aprovechamiento… **sin constituir
derechos reales sobre ellos**" [5], granted on a discretionary public-interest
standard, with a fine **up to the entire transaction value** for simulated acts
designed to circumvent it [5]. Treating "Mexico" as one screening unit is the
error to avoid.

**Greece — survives on ownership only by default**, because the corpus proves
nothing either way; every Greek tax-authority source refuses this run's fetch
service [64]. What *is* documented is a use-side restriction that specifically
penalises a purchaser: in the 1st, 2nd and 3rd districts of Athens, first-time
short-let registration is banned to 31 December 2026, and **property transferred
inter vivos is deleted from the registry and cannot re-register while the
restriction lasts** [25]. Buying a running short-let there destroys its
registration.

**Panama — the one country of the nine this corpus cannot support at all.** No
source establishes who may buy, under what instrument, or whether any border or
island carve-out exists. The land authority page 404'd, both Gaceta Oficial
fetches failed, and every Investment Climate Statement was inaccessible [63][68].
The macro profile that did land is cautionary: one rating agency has Panama at
**BB+, below investment grade** since 28 March 2024; debt about **70% of GDP**;
and the ITA-published summary names as impediments "corruption, insufficient
transparency and judicial capacity, **non-payment issues**, and an undereducated
workforce" [62]. Non-payment issues and weak judicial capacity go directly to
whether a lease is enforceable against a defaulting tenant.

On the evidence available, **Panama is the weakest of the nine and the one whose
inclusion is least supported**. That is a recommendation to resolve the gap
before proceeding, not a conclusion that Panama is unsuitable.

## The five mandated countries

**Hungary** is the only one of the nine where a US buyer faces a documented,
discretionary, per-property permit with a municipal-interest veto and mandatory
refusal grounds [3][4]. That is an execution risk with a price (HUF 65,000) and a
clock (45 days), not a bar — but it is a real gate, and the corpus gives no
approval-rate data.

**Costa Rica** bars a non-resident US buyer from the entire 200-metre coastal
strip and from islands, by statute rather than by permit [7]. Ley 6043 art. 47
closes the obvious workarounds too: entities domiciled abroad, entities formed in
Costa Rica by foreigners, and entities more than 50% foreign-owned are all
excluded, and share transfers in breach "carecerán de toda validez". The inland
regime — which is what most investors would actually buy — is **not evidenced by
this run**.

**Italy**'s gate is documented, and a treaty answer sits behind it: art.
VII(1)(b) of the 1949 US–Italy Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and Navigation
grants US citizens the right to acquire and own immovable property on conditions
no less favourable than Italians' [8]. Whether MAECI treats that as discharging
the Art. 16 condition is unconfirmed [1][2]. See
[purchase-mechanics.md](purchase-mechanics.md).

**France** has no source on foreign acquisition in this corpus at all. It was
user-mandated, so the action is to fetch the missing source, not to drop the
country.

**Spain** shows nothing restricting US ownership and nothing establishing that it
does not. What is evidenced is use-side and severe: Barcelona is extinguishing
the entire tourist-flat licence class by November 2028 [17][18], and the national
short-let registry was struck down by the Supreme Court in mid-2026 [16].

## One market-level screening finding

Peer-reviewed evidence that foreign buyers overpay [60]: across roughly 28,500
transactions in eight countries, "foreign investors pay significantly higher
prices than domestic investors, even after taking a wide variety of controls into
account", with the premium shrinking as the buyer's cumulative local experience
grows — and most foreign buyers sit below the experience threshold where it
disappears.

**The caveat is large enough that this cannot be used as a residential finding.**
The authors report that in the property-type split, for property types other than
industrial and office — **including apartments** — "the coefficients are
insignificant", reasoning that information asymmetry is weaker where values are
easier to measure. The dataset is institutional transactions above roughly US$1m,
and **France is the only one of the nine countries in it**.

Reported here as a directional caution for a first-time cross-border buyer, not
as a quantified residential result.

## Gaps

- Acquisition right: **six of nine** unestablished (France, Spain, Portugal,
  Greece, Panama, and Costa Rica inland).
- Geographic carve-outs for France, Spain and Greece: not addressed by any
  fetched file. Border or defence-zone restrictions on non-EU buyers may exist and
  were not tested.
- Market size and liquidity: no transaction-volume or days-on-market figure for
  any of the nine.
- Every Investment Climate Statement — the natural screening source for Costa
  Rica, Mexico and Panama — was inaccessible [63].
